input.idea: How to undo your last git commit without losing your changes: git reset --soft HEAD~1

template.reason: Most devs know the panic of committing too early. This template opens on that moment, then shows `git reset --soft HEAD~1` running in the terminal, with your changes still staged afterwards. It suits a faceless 30-second video, though the "tool" here is a single command, so "How-to steps" would also work if you want numbered steps.

hooks.text: Committed too early? Don't delete your work. Do this instead.
Saw a dev undoing his last commit like this
When you undo a git commit, you might think your changes vanish...

hook.text: Committed too early? Don't delete your work. Do this instead.

research.facts:
- `git reset --soft HEAD~1` removes your last commit, but your files and your staged changes stay exactly as they were. Git's docs say --soft leaves "your working tree files and the index unchanged."
- `HEAD~1` means "one commit before the one you're on now." Your branch moves back one step, and everything from the removed commit sits staged, so you can commit it again.
- Common uses: you wrote a typo in the commit message, or you forgot a file. Fix it, then run `git commit` again. Git's official docs give this exact "undo a commit and redo" example.
- Compare the modes: `--mixed` (the default) also keeps your files but unstages them. `--hard` overwrites your files to match the older commit, so any uncommitted work is lost.
- The same trick can squash several commits into one. Git's docs show `git reset --soft HEAD~5` followed by `git commit` to turn the last 5 commits into 1.
- If you already pushed the commit to a shared branch, the usual safer choice is `git revert`. It adds a new commit that undoes the old one, so nobody's history gets rewritten. Using reset there means you'd have to force-push.

scenes.voiceover: Committed too early? Don't delete your work. Do this instead.
scenes.onScreen: Committed too early? Don't delete your work.
scenes.visual: Animated git log graph: a fresh commit dot pops onto the branch with a red 'oops' badge; a trash can icon hovers nearby and gets crossed out

scenes.voiceover: You commit, then spot a typo or a forgotten file.
scenes.visual: Stylized terminal showing 'git commit -m "fix lgoin bug"'; the typo 'lgoin' gets circled in red, and a file icon 'auth.js' slides in labeled 'not committed'

scenes.voiceover: But reset --hard overwrites your files. Uncommitted work: gone.
scenes.visual: Terminal types 'git reset --hard HEAD~1'; code file cards beside it flash red and dissolve into dust

scenes.voiceover: Instead, use git reset --soft HEAD~1.
scenes.visual: The command types itself out in big monospace text on a dark terminal, '--soft' highlighted in green

scenes.voiceover: HEAD~1 means one commit back. Your branch steps back, and your changes stay staged.
scenes.onScreen: HEAD~1 = one commit back. Changes stay staged
scenes.visual: Commit graph: the HEAD/branch label slides back one dot; the removed commit's files fly into a green 'Staged' box, intact

scenes.voiceover: Fix the typo or add the file, then commit again.
scenes.visual: Terminal: 'git add auth.js' then 'git commit -m "fix login bug"'; a new clean commit dot appears on the graph with a green check

scenes.voiceover: Bonus: reset --soft HEAD~5, then commit, squashes five commits into one.
scenes.visual: Five small commit dots on the graph merge into one larger dot after 'git reset --soft HEAD~5' and 'git commit' appear in the terminal

scenes.voiceover: Files untouched. Already pushed to a shared branch? Use git revert instead.
scenes.visual: Split card: left a green shield over the files labeled 'local: reset --soft'; right a cloud icon labeled 'pushed: git revert' adding a new undo commit to the graph

prompt.system:
You are the producer of a short-video channel (TikTok, Reels, Shorts).
Your job in this step: choose how the video will be told, by picking ONE template
from the list you are given. You do not write the video yet.

You get the channel, the video idea and the templates.
Pick the template whose "when to use" fits the idea best; the length matters less.
A template's "needs" are the facts its required scenes are built on. Pick one the idea
can fill with its OWN facts: a rise-to-success story needs a success to show, a how-to
needs steps, a list needs items. If the idea lacks what a template needs, that template
does not fit, however close its topic is.
Never invent a template: answer only with an id from the list.
score: 5 = made for this idea and the idea has every fact it needs, 3 = workable,
1 = nothing in the list fits.
reason: one or two sentences for the creator, in plain English, about this idea.

prompt.system:
You write the script of a short vertical video (TikTok, Reels, Shorts).

Tell ONE connected story. The idea may be written as loose thoughts in any order: sort
them into the order the template's scenes tell (the problem before the fix, the cause
before the result), and let every scene follow from the one before it – the voiceovers
read in a row must make sense as one spoken text. A scene that promises something ("what I learned", "here's why") is
followed by the scene that says it.

The template is a guide: a structure that has worked for videos like this – its scenes,
their order and how they link. Follow it where it serves this idea; change the order,
leave a scene out or add one when that tells this story better. A "repeatable" scene
may appear several times in a row (one per step or item). Put every template scene you
leave out in "skipped" with a short reason.
A scene's "facts" come from the idea and the facts found online only – never invent a
tool, a number or a result.
When the idea has no fact for a scene, leave it out if it is optional; if it is required,
fill it with what the idea does say rather than with an invented claim.
Its "creative" parts are yours to word.

The first scene is the hook: say the chosen hook as it is, and show its key words.
The template's links ("→ next") and the transition phrases are examples of how scenes
can follow each other; use them only where they read naturally. End the way that fits
this video best: the CTA formulas show endings that have worked – use one, or write
your own, or none if no ending asks for one.
The call to action never sends people to a link, a website, a download or a giveaway
the idea does not mention – then pick a CTA formula that needs none of those.

For every scene:
- voiceover: what is said, natural spoken English
- onScreen: the key words shown big, not the whole sentence
- visual: what the viewer sees, concrete (a terminal running a command, a settings page,
  an app icon), never "something engaging"
- needsRecording: your call – true when the scene is shown best with the creator's own
  screen recording rather than a picture the video editor draws.

Keep within the limits. Each scene lasts about as long as its voiceover: fill the wanted
length – add more steps or items with the repeatable scenes, keep the optional scenes
that help – rather than stopping short.

Scenes:
- opening / hook (2–2.8 s): Shows or states the wrong way people do it. [required] → next: contrast; facts: pain; creative: who

- sequence: First, | Second, | Third, | First is | Second is | Third is
- contrast: But | Instead | Instead of just | But instead, | but in reality, | but that's not how
- bridge: So if you want | So just | To get the full | For a PDF | So want to try it for yourself? | Now you might be wondering...
- open-loop-payoff: It's called | You have probably heard of | Here's the easiest way | All roads lead to Rome... | And that's why... | Anthropic just dropped

CTA formulas (types allowed: none):
- none: end on the last scene, without a call to action (skip the cta scene)

Limits, from the analysis of successful videos:
- speak at most 3.4 words per second
- a scene lasts at most 9 s, the hook at most 5 s
- at most 15 words on screen in a scene

- If you already pushed the commit to a shared branch, the usual safer choice is `git revert`. It adds a new commit that undoes the old one, so nobody's history gets rewritten. Using reset there means you'd have to force-push.

Face on camera: no, a faceless video
Motion graphics only: no recordings at all (needsRecording is always false).
